ig_caption:
Four openings worth learning first: two for White, two for Black.

The Italian Game and the London System give White quick development and an easy plan. Against 1.e4, the Caro-Kann keeps Black solid; against 1.d4, the Queen's Gambit Declined holds the centre without fuss. None of them depends on a trap, so they keep working as you climb.

Which one do you play already, and which would you add? 👇

slides.title: Four openings
slides.sub: TWO FOR WHITE, TWO FOR BLACK
slides.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5

slides.title: Italian Game
slides.moves: e4 e5 Nf3 Nc6 Bc4 Bc5
slides.take: Knight out, bishop out, castle. The bishop on c4 aims at f7, the weakest square in Black's camp.
slides.edge: The plan: c3 and d4 to take the centre. Natural moves, and every one of them has a reason.

slides.title: London System
slides.moves: d4 d5 Bf4 Nf6 e3 e6 Nf3 Bd6 Bg3
slides.take: The same set-up against almost anything: d4, Bf4, e3, Nf3. Less theory, more time to think in the middlegame.
slides.edge: The habit it teaches: keep the dark-squared bishop outside the pawn chain before you play e3.

slides.title: Caro-Kann
slides.moves: e4 c6 d4 d5 Nc3 dxe4 Nxe4 Bf5
slides.take: 1…c6 and 2…d5 build a solid centre. The light-squared bishop comes out to f5 before e6 locks it in.
slides.edge: Why it suits climbing players: few early tactics against you, and a healthy pawn structure into the endgame.

slides.title: Queen’s Gambit Declined
slides.moves: d4 d5 c4 e6 Nc3 Nf6 Bg5 Be7
slides.take: 2…e6 keeps the pawn on d5 supported. Black develops, castles and breaks with …c5 or …e5 later.
slides.edge: The point: you don't need to win the c4 pawn. Hold the centre and the position stays sound.
